nodes.name: Reindeer lichen
nodes.desc: A pale ground lichen of tundra and open spruce woods. Wikipedia calls it the favourite food of caribou, which dig through snow to reach it.

nodes.name: Black crowberry
nodes.desc: A low evergreen tundra shrub with black berries that ptarmigan, caribou and other animals eat, as recorded in GloBI.

nodes.name: Bog bilberry
nodes.desc: A tundra berry shrub. Wild blueberries are a main part of the bears' diet in Denali, and caribou, ptarmigan and ground squirrels also eat the plant or fruit.

nodes.name: Willows
nodes.desc: Shrubs of lowland and tundra that moose browse, according to the park service. Hares, ptarmigan, ground squirrels and Dall sheep eat them too.

nodes.name: Fireweed
nodes.desc: A tall pink wildflower of open and disturbed ground that blooms through summer and feeds bumble bees, per GloBI records.

nodes.name: Caribou
nodes.desc: Eats lichens, especially in winter, plus tundra berry shrubs. Denali held about 2,200 in a 2013 survey, according to Wikipedia.

nodes.name: Moose
nodes.desc: Browses on willow in the park's lowlands and is prey for wolves and grizzlies.

nodes.name: Dall sheep
nodes.desc: Grazes grasses, sedges and willow on steep alpine slopes, using lichens and mosses in winter. Denali was founded in part to protect the sheep.

nodes.name: Arctic ground squirrel
nodes.desc: Eats willows, berries, seeds and some insects and stores food for winter. Predators include foxes, wolves, bears, lynx and eagles.

nodes.name: Snowshoe hare
nodes.desc: A browser of shrubs and twigs whose numbers rise and fall in cycles. It is the main prey of the Canada lynx and food for many other predators.

nodes.name: Willow ptarmigan
nodes.desc: A ground bird of tundra and shrubland that eats berries, buds and willow, and is prey for foxes, wolves, lynx and eagles.

nodes.name: Bumble bees
nodes.desc: Many bumble bee species are recorded in the park. They feed on nectar and pollen from fireweed and other wildflowers.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: A clever scavenger and omnivore that feeds on carrion left by wolves and bears, as well as berries and small prey.

nodes.name: Red fox
nodes.desc: The park service shows foxes hauling Arctic ground squirrels back to the den. Also eats hares, ptarmigan and berries.

nodes.name: Canada lynx
nodes.desc: A hare specialist. Snowshoe hares can make up most of its diet, and lynx numbers follow the hare cycle. Rarely seen in Denali.

nodes.name: Golden eagle
nodes.desc: Abundant in Denali. Takes ground squirrels, hares, ptarmigan and Dall sheep lambs, and also feeds on carrion.

nodes.name: Gray wolf
nodes.desc: Hunts caribou, moose, Dall sheep and hares. Wikipedia counted about 51 wolves in 13 packs in 2014.

nodes.name: Grizzly bear
nodes.desc: Eats mostly berries in summer but also takes caribou, moose and ground squirrels, and scavenges carcasses.

nodes.name: Summer sunlight
nodes.desc: Long summer days power a short, intense growing season on the tundra.

nodes.name: Snowpack and meltwater
nodes.desc: Winter snow insulates low shrubs and hares, and the spring melt waters the tundra.

nodes.name: Permafrost
nodes.desc: Wikipedia describes the park's permafrost as discontinuous and the shallow permafrost as thawing. Frozen ground limits tree growth and holds water near the surface.

nodes.name: Thin tundra soil
nodes.desc: Cold, thin soils keep most trees and shrubs small, according to Wikipedia.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, dung and carcasses slowly in the cold, returning nutrients to the soil.
